The "AVIS." Christiansted , Friday the 16 <A March 1S55. Slraiu roniimmicalioii between this Island nrul St. Thomas, is, we consider, very desirable and would be of much importance to these islands. We wonder why this desideratum has not been accomplished ere this, and feel surprised to notice that it has remained so long dormant. We therefore offer a few brief remarks on the subject, which may not be out of place. Some time ago the matter was warmly spoken of, and, we believe, a steamer was even put on trial, but was afterwards found not to answer the purpose. Since then nothing more has been heard of it and the project seems forgotten. The facilities of steam communication are great and too well known to need much comment ; and the pecuniary advantages derived from such a source are clearly developed in commercial places, and among men of enterprise. It is, however, the opinion of some persons that a steamer could not pay its expenses here, as the number of passengers bet ween these two islands would not offer sufficient guarantee, nor would the amount of freight be adequate. This idea seems erroneous as it is the general belief that if a steamer were plying between this and St. Thomas, the contrary would be the result. The facility offered to passengers would increase the number, as detention on account of contrary winds and calm weather would be obviated þÿ thus pecuniary advantages would accrue and the enterprise be fully appreciated. Ilere, again, is another consideration. The steamercould make tripson Sundays and other Holy Days, and it would af-

ford people an opportunity to see their relatives and friends on such days, who from their avocations are otherwise prevented ; or to take a trip for recreation. By such means as these and performing the Government's service, for which, no doubt, a fair sum would be given, there is every reason to suppose that the enterprise would pay þÿ and we think that the subject is worthy the consideration of capitalists to engage in, and thereby promote the interest and welfare of these islands.

Value of Printing. þÿ In 1274 the price of a small bible, neatly translated, was £30, a sum equal to at least £300 of our money. A good and clear printed bible may mow be had for two or three shillings. It is related that the building the two arches of London-bridge cost only £15, which is £5 less than what a copy of the bible sold for many years afterwards. These facts afford a curious commentary on the change and advantages produced by the extraordinary invention of printing, which has done so much to alter all the institutions of the world wherever the press has appeared.

Yesterday the Comptroller for Transport Service forwarded a notice to Lloyd's, intimating an augmentation of the fleet of transports, furnishing the numbers" of the additional vessels hired hy the Government, hy which we find that almost every steamship in the merchant service has been taken up for the purposes of the war. The transport fleet now muster no fewer than 200 ships of the largest class, upwards of a third of which are propelled hy steam. The leviathan Great Britain is under orders to s.iil for the Crimea next week. She is fitting up for about 1,050 infantry and 30 horses. Her capabilities for taking out stores and ammunition are too well known to need remark. The iEtna screw \ steamer, and the Telegraph steamer will in all probability leave Liverpool about the same time; the former will take out stores and 170 horses, and the latter 120 commissary drivers and stores. By telegraph yesterday we learn that the Imperador screw transport had reached Cork, and was taking on hoard detachments of the 1st Royals and of the 43th Regiment, in all about 1.000 men, for Balaklava. The fitling-up of this ship to suit the comfort of the men is highly spoken of, f each man being provided with a long

hammock anil bedding, &c. The Himalaya screw steamship hourly expected at Woolwich dockyard to take out 400 horses, several large mortars, gnus, ammunition, stores, provisions, arid two companies of the Royal Horse Artillery. The Siinwdon transport, vviili the lust batch of wooden lints on hoard, and the men from the London Docks, to act as waifingers at Balaklava, has sailed. I lie Croesus, Harbinger, or one of the other newly-numbered steam transports, will, in all probability, take out, in the course of the ensuing week, one of the Militia regiments to Malta.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session. Report to llis Hajestj. In consequence of the draft of an ordinance relative to medical attendance on estates, the regulations of which being different for each of the islands, the Colonial Council would first state our

- 3 T I 0 m » O X A T J 3 opinion with regard to the first part relating to St. Croix. During the discussions in the Council it has been elucidated, that most of the sugar estates in St. Croix are provided with medical attendance; the physician is either engaged by the owner of the estate for a fixed pay annuallly, or for the amount which is weekly retained out of the wages of those laborers, who can afford such deduction, generally 2 stivers pr week from each ; þÿ or engaged by the laborers jointly, in which latter case however the same amount is generally retained weekly by the manager, and paid to the physician. Finally, that on several estates there exists no arrangement with any physician, but who requires medical assistance and cannot go to the physician, procures the visit of a physician either himself or through the means of his family, in which case, as far as we can It arn, the remuneration for the doctor's travelling expenses is paid in advance. Medicines are generally always furnished by the estate without any remuneration, and at times by the physician employed. Thus, as far as regards the sugar-estates in St. Croix we take it for granted, that there already exist þÿ fprobably especially in consequence of the arrangement of those relations previous to the emancipation) þÿ satisfactory arrangements in this respect to a greater extent, than we are aware is the case in any other colony. Moreover venereal and other cases are treated at the hospitals in Christiansted and Frederiksted without being paid

for, and patients suffering from certain injuries are by order of the King's Physician (LaudphysicusJ laid up at the siekhouse erected for that purpose at the St. Croix prison; þÿ furthermore, in conformity ! with the provisional ordinance of26th Jany. 1849 17, on estates where no physician is engaged, the following rule is observed, that in ease of dangerous illness and the patient being helpless, the estate is bound to procure medical aid. There are 9 medical practitioners in the island, out of which the 3 are appointed by public authority, and 2 apothecaries. Under these circumstances, and considering also that the island is a healthy place of reridence, especially with regard to the natives; that those remedies applied in common cases of sickness are simple, well known and easily obtained ; that the most deplorable cases, say the disproportionate number of deaths among little children, are not to be attributed to the want of medical aid, but on the contrary to the gross neglect of the mothers ; the Colonial Council are of opinion, that there is no reason for enacting any compulsory law with regard to medical attendance, least of all any exceptional compulsory law for the one half of the populatation of the island living on the sugar estates. A law of that nature would be void of foundation in justice, and moreover give rise to many practical inconveuiences, among which we j Fire occurred towards will state some. ! Tt would certainly have been desirable had the planters and physicians, during the first period af-

ter emancipation, agreed upon medical attendance on estates for a fixed pay, as there scarcely at that time would have been made difficulties on the part of the laborers with regard to a moderate deduction in their wages ; hut even at the emanation of the provisional ordinance there was so far from existing any unanimity among the parties concerned, that it was considered a matter of hesitation to encroach on the relations with any dictatorial regulation ; but it was expected that partly the competition for rendering the condition of the laborers on each estate just as comfortable as on the neighbouring one, partly the interest of the parties concerned in a pecuniary respect would bo a sufficient enticement to secure regular medical attendance in cases where the proprietor or the laborer might feel the want of it. Since that time the devclopcment. of the relations has made it still more inexpedient to apply coercive means in this respect ; tho planters are obliged above all to avoid disagreement with tho I possible inquiries laborers, especially as regards personal relations ; when the people on an estate, where no physician has hitherto been engaged, objeot to employ one, for instance : in cases where one family use one physician and another family another physician or a number of them will not have a
. certain physician, then the law, that cannot aid the planter in procuring the necessary force of labor ought not involve on him such occasions of loss of labor. (To be continued.)

The "AVIS." Christiansted, Tuesday the 20 th March 1S5G. We have frequently seen at night a strong light on the reef running along the bay of Princess and Golden Rock, or thereabout, and upon inquiry discovered that ceitain persons n sort thither with torches for the purpose of fishing. Now, whatever benefit may accrue to such persons by this means, we think it rather a dangerous expedient ; lor vessels running between this and St. Thomas, on their course in ward, might easily mistake such a light for one ot those on shore, and thereby be decoyed on the reef. No doubt a prohibition of such a practice would he deemed a serious wrong by those in the habit, yet we must express it as our opinion, that if such were the case a source of danger to our traders would he removed, and the apparent wrong being the lesser of two evils, would be of little weight when compared with the great risk and danger which is insured i>y the said practice.

From the St. Thomas Times , March 14. The Fire ! ! ! At Four o'clock on Sunday afternoon a Fire was discovered in the substantial brick building No. 34, in the Main Street þÿ on the first floor of which was kept tho front Store of Messrs. Win :more <$- Co., and where the Fire originated. tho second floor was occupied as the Custom House, Burgher Council's Office, Post Office, Harbor Master's Office, and Notary's Office. Only by considerable exertion were the Books and Re mds of those Offices preserv cd from falling a prey to the flames, and suggests to the observer l.uw very necessary it is that buildiugs requited for the use of important Public Offices of the kind should be properly erected for them , so that vaults could he introduced in order to secure their Archives in the moment of danger. "We are led to these remarks from the correctness of the opinion which is generally expressed that had tho evening or night the opportunity would not have offered to rescue a single book or document from either of those Offices The tolling of the alarm bell at the Fort announced to the inhabitants that a Fire had broken out in the city, and the volumes of smoke rising in the air pointed out the locality. After a little while the Fort and Town Engines were dragged to the spot, as also one or two private ones. For a time there was a difficulty to procure water, but by the invariable good services of the women þÿ who never fail to serve well and faithfully at such critical times þÿ a supply was obtained It soon became clear to every one that

the building and its contents þÿ which happened to be merchandize stored almost to excess þÿ must be consumed, and attention became directed to those points where a probability existed of the fire spreading. Fortunately, however, the vicinity is so thoroughly fire-proof that the devouring element was completely confined to the one building. The proprietors and tenants of the adjoining stores and dwellings were, nevertheless, extremely alarmed and concerned to know the probable fate of the amount of wealth and property which at that moment were lying exposed to the fickle and capricious march of tho treacherous element. Therefore, many were the anxious made as to whether it would be to control and keep the fire within the narrow sphere where it commenced. As time wore on tho excitement became more intense, and towards evening the fire having reached the roof of the building þÿ which was covered with tile it fell in, after (he flames had attained their highest point and the rafters reduced to cinders. A better feeling succeeded, and confidence as-

sumed the place of doubt and fear, þÿ as it was i then observable that the fire, if properly watched, could not extend. The amount of property con- i sumed in the Stores of Messrs. Whitmore <Wo. is variously estimated þÿ some say Sixty, others Eighty, and others again go as high as One Hundred Thousand Dollars; but we are inclined to suppose that $80,000 may be taken as the maximum loss. No insurance had been effected on any portion of the property, which was of a varied character. It is gratifying to say that the Books and valuable Papers of the firm were saved, having been placed into two large Salamanders, of the manufacture of St las 0. Herring, New York, and were visited by numbers on the following day to satisfy their curiosity as to the quality of those Safes as non-conductors of heat, and their capacity of preserving anything that might be put within them. Of the origin of the Fire we believe public opinion is tolerably well formed that it was the result of "spontaneous combustion," particularly as it occurred at a time when the Store had been closed for a longer period (24 hours) than on any previous occasion since it had been so closely packed. The want of circulation of air must have engendered a heat of many degrees beyond the usual range of the Thermometer, and great enough to ignite any article which possessed such a tendency. A smoking continues to rise from the smouldering remains of the merchandize now lying within the walls of the Store, like a mound of earth

temporarily thrown up, or closer resembling au immense dung-heap composed of damaged tobacco (leaf and junk), pork, beef, wooden clocks, ware, dying stuffs, cordage, remains oakutn, rice, canvas, tinware and hard- of oil cans, boxes, barrels, hogsheads, and other articles too numerous to detail. An Engine, with a hose leading from the sea, stands in readiness at the door with i the discharge pipe carried into the building, saturating the rubbish as circumstances call for, and box carts are busily engaged removing this collection of matter, once constituting wealth and riches, but now valueless, and expensive to begot rid of As far as we can judge it will occupy many days yet before the premises can be thoroughly cleared away, þÿ meanwhile obstructing all business in the immediate neighbourhood ; we are, nevertheless, grateful that things have been no worse. The thanks of the Public are do. to the Commanders of the Royal Mail Steam Ships Tyne and Eagle for the valued Crews rendered by their Officers, Engineers, services and Firemen on Sunday night þÿ also to the Captains of Merchantmen in port who acted in like manner. We have also to acknowledge the use of the R. M. Company's Engines from their Coal Depot.

DEFEAT OF THE RUSSIANS AT EUPATOR1A, BY OMAR PASHA BUCHAREST, Friday. þÿ A messenger left Eupatoria on the 20th Feb., and performed the journey from Varna to Bucharest in 2G hours, brings the following despatch : þÿ " Eupatoria, Feb. 18. þÿ The Russians attacked Eupatoria this morning. They were commanded by Liprandi ; and their numbers were 40,000. They commenced the attack an hour before daybreak, and had with them seventy guns. " The conflict lasted four hours. The assault was signally repulsed. The steamers threw shells among the assailants. The Russians have 500 men hors die combat, the Turks 150 " Omar Pasha commanded in person. " Suleyman Pasha, the Egyptian, was killed. " Masses of cavalry and artillery are now assembled round Eupatoria." The Turks had 15 men killed and 35 wounded. The French manned one of the defensive batteries on shore, and lost five men. The ships co-operated effectively in repelling the Russian attack

PROCEEDINGS OF THE COLONIAL COUNCIL Second Session Report to His Tlajesty. (Continued) Such a law does in reality not conferany right to the planter ; it may, it is true, compel him to pay

vices, or to remain on an estate where they imagine they are wronged. For the information of those not acquainted with our local relations, it may yet be observed, that the laborers are from old times extremely suspicious with regard to the engagement of phyas is uot paid for the purpose prescribing of medicines, hut for issuing certificates whether alleged indisposition is real or feigned ; it is a known fact, that on several occasions attempts made to employ physicians without the consent of the laborers have given rise to great disturbances and loss to the respective estates, withont arriving at any better result. Just as insignificant as the right of the planter to engage a physician according to such a compulsory law would be, just so would be his right to retain 3 cents weekly out of the wages of the laborer. When the laborers are not accustomed to, and will not allow any such deduction applied for the purposes, in their opinion useless or even degrading, tho planter will prefer paying also these, perhaps to the amount of, $ 60 or $ 70 annually out of his own pocket, than to be exposed to receive warning of removal from the laborers, who cannot be replaced. þÿ And if one of the proprietor yields þÿ which with certainty may be foreseen will take place þÿ it will be a point of honor for the laborers of the neighbouring estate to enforce the same right. Viewed from this side the case appears similar to a new law of taxation. I3e it further observed, that according to the de

velopment of the relations of labor in St. Croix, it cannot bo deemed possible to enforce the deduction in question without the consent of both parties When tbo draft exceptionally mentions þÿ sugar þÿestates, it will from the existing relations he uncertain, what estates are to be included in that denomination Not a few of former sugar-estates become gradually dismantled, or if they are partially in sugar cultivation, the crop is taken off on another property belonging to the same or another proprietor, þÿ moreover some so called stockestates have more domiciled people than several sugar-estates As the relations arc at present left to the free agreement between the parties that are to pay and those that are to receive, the question what services the physician is to render, naturally regulates itself according to what is necessary and useful. On many estates the agreement is, that the physician shall visit the estate once a week, generally in the commencement of tho week ; otherwise when sent for, on others, especially the smaller and more distant estates, he only visits the estate when called, which may-be does not happen once every second month Rut what extent of duty is incumbent on the physician is not concontained in the proposed obligation on the proprietor þÿ to engage a physician by contract þÿ? It is evident that no general rule can be fixed, and as matters are situated, it would mostly be left to the physician himself to decide, what þÿ attenþÿdance would be considered sufficient

On the estates in St. Croix there is a great number of people, who, although generally classed among the laborers, are neither laborers nor belonging to the þÿlaborers families; according to the draft no provisions are made to secure medical attendance to them, notwithstanding measures of a sanitary nature ought to apply to them as well as to individuals working on the estates. The same observations are applicable to tho population on stook-estates ; especially as on these there is not that guarantee for order and cleanliness and speedy assistance in case of illness, which is at hand more or less on all sugar estates, in consequenoe of their organisation. The circumstances stated above have determin- 'd the Colonial Council to disrecommend the said

regulations in the draft ; to which view of the case wo have been led by a more general consideration of the matter, because a law concerning a compulsory payment from one class of traders to another (and the latter including but few individuals) would be a breach of principles, which could not be put aside without called for by quite extraordinary circumstances, in cases of actual necessity, but none such are present here. A compulsory payment would make the position of only one of the parties somewhat favorable, while the other, the planter, would be placed in a new relation of dependence not only with regard to the apparent co-contractor, but also to others, who in this relation have no responsibility whatever, viz., the laborers. Whatever modifications such a regulation might receive, would only be palliatives, if f. i. in order to obviate possible combinations there should be proposed, to make the obligation to þÿ engage a physician by conþÿtract dependent that such a physician could be had for a certain minimum for each individual. Such a clause would in the first place establish a class of sugar estates exempted, by which means the law, which at any rate ought to have some general foundation, would embrace even a less number of estates and persons ; in the next place it would occasion, that those estates which no physician with extensive practice could attend to at a fixed pay, would eventually bo compelled to engage the service of practitioners, who are otherwise not sought.

On Monday and Tuesday it became generally known that serious differences of opinion existed amongst members of the Cabinet as to the way in which Mr. þÿRoebuck motion, s nominating his committeo of inquiry into the calamities of the war, should be aiet On Tuesday night, after tho meeting of the Cabinet, it was stated that these differences had become so serious as to be irreconcileable and on Wednesday morning, both at the West-end and in the City, that there was little doubt of the resignation of Sir James Graham, Mr Sidney Herbert, and Mr. Gladstone. OPINIONS or tut PRESS on the CABINET CRISIS The Morning Chronicle. The announcement made on Thursday evening by L<vd Palmerston in the House of þÿCommons hat three members of his Administration, tilling most important offices, had resigned þÿ will be received with much regret by the country. The position in whioh we are placed þÿ as it were, between the certainty of war and the formal anticipation of peace þÿ makes us even more than usually sensible, at the present moment, of the

3 ti\ 8 Ji D A T II loss we sustain by being deprived of the services of such distinguished statesmen, and such able administrative officers. The Chancellor of the Exchequer, the Secretary of state for the Colonies, and the First Lord of the Admiralty only hold their offices till their successors are appointed ; and it is no flattery to those right honourable gentlemen to affirm, that to replace them will be extremely difficult. Into the causes which induced Mr. Gladstone, Sir James Graham, and Mr. Sidney Herbert to resign, it is not necessary here to enter. Some of our contemporaries have hazarded oracular statements of the circumstances that have led to this result, and it is possible that the country may have received with confidence their assurances If, on the surface of things their is the wherewithal to suggest, there is not enough to justify, this mode of expounding the motives of Cabinet Ministers, when, according to the practice of the constitution, those motives ought only to be disclosed in the manner prescribed by Parliamentary law and usage. For our own p rt, we think it more respectful alike to the Sovereign, to the Parliament, and to the outgoing Ministers, to await the authentic version which those right honourable gentlemen will give in their places in Parliament. The Premier has informed the country, through tho House of Commons, that those explanations will be given this evening; and until then, even the most correct guessing, or the most indiscreet confidences, must alike be hazarded without the stamp of

j authority. It is in no invidious spirit that we have referred to the difficulty of replacing the gentlemen who have resigned There are men of talent , and influence, of experience, and of undoubted political probity, who will, in all probability, be found to fill the places now vacated. The nation, therefore, has no reason to be discouraged But it would be scarcely respectful to the public, with whose almost unanimous approval those exmembers of the Palmerston Administration have for so long a time conducted the business of some of the most important departments of tho State, not to recall their antecedents, or to insist upon their merits and past services. Of the Chancellor of the Exchequer it may be said, that during his administration of the Exchequer, he established principles which must ever form the basis of any sound financial system in this country. As far removed from pedantic adherence to tradition as from the rashness of modern theorists, he has demonstrated that boldness is compatible with safety, even in experimental fiscal legislation. A machinery constructed for a period of peace, has been found elastic enough to meet the demands of a formidable war ; and the means have been pointed out of sustaining the military dignity of the country, without alarming the just sensibility of modern economists, lest we should be led into a repetition of former extravagance. Of the oratorical powers of Mr. Gladstone, and his admirable qualities as a Parliamentary leader,

it is unnecessary to remind the reader. It is not likely that those distinguishing characteristics of the right honourable gentleman will be allowed to fall into abeyance, because circumstances have induced him to think it consistent with his duty to quit the present Administration

From the Observer , April 29, 1855. SUMMARY OF THE BOMBARD- MENT OF SEBASTOPOL. The fire of our batteries opened at five o'clock a. m. on the 9th, and the Russians, who were taken by surprise, did not reply for 20 minutes, which was of great advantage to us, as it enabled us to make our aim more certain. During the whole of the 9th, notwithstanding an incessant rain, the cannonade continued on both sides with extraordinary vigour. Towards six p. in. the Russians ceased their fire, and during the whole night only threw out a few shells. Their aim. in the beginning, was very uncertain, it subsequently improved, and is now pretty fair. The rain, which filled our trenches with mud, greatly annoyed us, as our heavy guns backing after each shot damaged the platforms on which they stand. A little after six our cannonade was suspended, and a shower of bombs, shells, and congreve rockets was poured into the town until daylight. Our loss during that day was inconsiderable. The batteries suffered little, a few embrasures only being slightly damaged. The whole was repaired during the night. On the side of the Russians, the top of the Flagstaff Bastion was entirely carried away ; the forts of the Quarantine half destroyed ; the Central Bastion strongly damaged ; and the Barrack batteries, torn up by our cannon balls and shells, kept up but a slow and uncertain fire. The barracks situate behind them received all the projectiles that passed over those batteries and were also considerably injured ; and the foot-bridge, which connects the two
quarters of the city, was repeatedly struck 'our cannon balls. Unfortunately, uight came on two hours too

© IR © St £ ATK soon. The next morning, the Russians had removed the bridge 200 yards lower down, beyond the reach of our guns. During the night of the 9th, nothing remarkable occurred, but we suffered great hardships in the trenches, where we were up to our knees in water. Our fire, nevertheless, did not cease one instant. At four o'clock on the morning of the 10th, the Russians recommenced their fire with rage. They spent the night in repairing their casualties ; the weather continued bad, and the rain was incessant. The terrible duel of artillery was in the meantime maintained on both sides, until night, without any material result. At three in the afternoon the enemy had only three guns available in the tower of Malakhoff, eight or ten in the Barrack batteries, three or four in the Central Bastion, two in the Flagstaff Battery, and about 15 along the entire line of the Quarantine. At six o'clock their fire sensibly slackened, when we began to shell the town with redoubled vigour. No less than 80 bombs were seen at a time in the air, falling on the town and batteries. The enemy attempted three sorties, but was repulsed each time. At two o'clock in the morning of the lltli, fires broke out in several parts of the city. At five the Russian batteries, which had remained nearly silent during the night, re-opened with vigour, but the number of their guns had visibly decreased. The fire was kept up during the whole of the 11th, when the entire front of the fort of the Quarantine was levelled with

the ground, and all the guns of the Flagstaff Bastion, excepting one mortar, were silenced. The fire of the Central Bastion was slow and uncertain. The rain ceased, and the weather became fine. At ten o'clock p. m., 1,200 French, provided with pickaxes, shovels, and earth bags, scaled the parapet, in order to open, on the right of the Flagstaff Bastion, a trench, connecting the T with the third parallel. The Russians made a powerful sortie in that direction, advancing in close columns upon the partv, who fired into them a murderous volley, and charging them at the point of the bayonet drove them into a ravine. The enemy returned three times to the charge, with as little success. They then opened a fire of grape-shot with three fieldpieces they had contrived to place in position on the declivity of the Flagstaff Bastion, which occasioned some casualties. The trench was. nevertheless, executed under that fire. The Dcneral of Engineers, Bizot was, however, wounded by a musket ball in the neck. Next day the English again set the town on fire in several places with Congreve rockets. The allies shelled the town during the whole night of the 1 1th. The foot-bridge, which the Russians had removed, was broken in two places by our bombs, so that the communication between the two-quarters of the place is entirely intercepted. The Russians attempted three sorties to the left, of the T, but were repulsed with considerable loss. At six o'clock a. m. on the 12th

the fire slackened by degrees, and ultimately subsided, when there was a sort of truce for a few hours. The Malakhoff Tower and its batteries, which were observed to be in a ruined state, were completely silent. At ten o'clock a. m. the firing recommenced, and lasted the whole day ; at night, however, it was feebly kept up. On the 13th, the fire of the Quarantine, in the right of the city, was nearly extinguished. The Southern Bastion was silent and greatly damaged. Forts Constantino, Catherine, and Quarantine showed no sign of life.

A Receipt for Getting a Husband. þÿ 1 he following simple nnd expeditious meihod of acquiring a husband, we clip from an English paper, ll is a receipt which is said to be almost invariably efficacious. and we recommend it to the consideration of lady aspirants for jovs matrimonial, who are beyond a certain age : þÿ " A gentleman of the bar in a neighbouring country in easy circumstances and pretty good practice, had rendered himself somewhat remarkable bv his attempts in the way of matrimonial speculation. A maiden rather advanced in years, residing some miles distant in the neighbourhood, hearing of litis lawyer's speculating propensity, lhat his character was unexceptionable, and his situation in life was tolerably good, resolved upon making him her husband. She hit upon the following expedient : She pretended suddenly to bo taken very ill, and sent for the man of ihe law to prepare her will. He atlended for that purpose. By her will she devised JbfO,- 000 in bank stock to be divided among her three cousins, some thousands in bonds ann notes to a niece, nnd a vast landed estate to a favourite nephew. The will being finished, she gave her lawyer a very liberal lee, ami enjoined secrecy upon him for Some pretended purpose, thus precluding him from an in quiry into her real circumstances. Need I mention ihe result? In a foi might the lady thought proper to he again reston I m health, The lawyer called lo congratulate her on her restoration þÿ begged permission to visit her,

which was politely given. After a shoit courtship, the desired nfler was made 1 he bargain was concluded and ratified by ihe priest. The lawyer's whole estate by his wife consists of an annuity of sixiv-five dol lars."

From the St. Thomas Times, May 12. T1IE WEEK. town at the present time þÿ Quiet arid calmness reign supreme in our not even an ' Election' being able to remove the monotonous mood into which the public, from dullness in trade and a want of arrivals to impart fresh intelligence, seem to have relapsed. The election, which was fixed for yesterday, it is now clear has, after passing its calminating point on previous occasions, sunk in this instance below all parallel. Not a voter appeared at the poll to record his vote. Here, then, we behold an indignity offered to a sacred privilege, which in past times, and in other countries, drove men to the most prodigious extremes. Is it that our Institutions are so perfect that no feature of change will be ventured upon ? No ! But, doubtless, the champions and idolators of the absolutist principle will proclaim it so ! However, the reason we all know is patent. The inhabitants of St. Thomas are no longer indifferent to the consequences of giving life to a Council by a spirited election, which could only return members to an Assembly where, from innumerable causes, we could only exhibit an unequal position, even supposing proper members were obtainable. With a larger constituency than St. Croix we are allowed to return nix members, while that Island enjoys eight, and four members of its community, in most cases, have been chosen by the Government to represent the Crown. Admitting that the Council enjoyed rare prerogatives ; that it was legislative instead of consultative, by which it

would be susceptible of greater action ; we would experience the pleasing thought of being met by twelve for our six members. We hope that the Government of Denmark, having conceded to us the right of asking for a separate Council, and which we must be permitted to say should have been claimed by our first six members, will yet extend to us that advantage which we fear in the first instance we permitted to be lost. Supposing we enjoyed a separate Council, and our condition changed, we can undertake to aver, that " Election Day" in St. Thomas would possess those features of excitement and interest so manifest in almost every country where a Franchise exists.

In no community, it is our belief, does the abominable evil of defamation exist to such an extent, as in this small one of ours. The private character of an individual, he it never so bright and unspotted, is no proof against the slanderous tongue of as diabolical a crew as ever existed on the face of this earth. Maiden innocence blushes at the immoral and indecent slanders heard on the very streets. Within the last days some individuals, who, to judge from the language employed, must he of the lowest scum, which it is the misfortune of any community to he burdened with, have scandalously put forth a number of letters in which the characters of individuals have been falsely and maliciously assailed. The venomous shafts of these monstrosities have been aimed at every one, no doubt with the intention of leaving mortal marks, which time could, perhaps, with difficulty efface. Hut this has not been effected. Their object has failed through their very grossness and palpable falsehood. We were almost of opinion, that these effusions were too low to he noticed in our columns; hut in the hope that condign punishment may be indicted on the foul-mouthed slanderers, we have been tempted to allude to the subject. Better would it he for these individuals had they devoted their misused time to the study of their spelling books ; and we would advise all who thirst for notoriety, even at the risk of shameful punishment, that whenever they are seized with a rage for scrib-

ling, and are tempted to rush boldly on in a field for which neither education nor habits fit them, to dip their rude pens in water, so that their obscene language may be dissipated in the air and not left to stain the paper as well as the reputation of persons. Wo trust that these individual may be discovered, and made an example of ; for, we have around us a host of similar characters, who possessing "a little learning," that "dangerous thing" may be induced to attempt at some future time a like course.

From the Observer, April 22, 1855. FRENCH STATE PAPER ON THE WAR þÿ No. II. "As regards ilic conditions of peace, nothing can be more just, more moderate, more conformable to the rights and interests of Europe. It will be easy for us to establish this by characterizing clearly the thought which dictated them, and the object which they were to achieve. The lirst of the four conditions, in putting an end to the protectorate of Russia, in the principalities of Moldavia, Wallachia, and Servia, and in placing their privileges under the collective guarantee of the Great Fowers, takes away from the Cabinet of St. Petersburg the rights which it pretended to hold from ancient treaties, and whicli were only the means for subjugating those populations, for dominating Turkey, for approaching Austria on Iter most vulnerable side, and lor troubling the whole of

Europe ; the second by stipulating the free navigation of the Danube, liberates the commerce of all nations þÿ especially of Austria þÿ from the moral and material obstacles which impede it, and throws open the mouths of that great river to the states of which it is the fortune and the defence. " The fourth, in delivering Turkey from the pretensions of Russia to a religious protectorate over the Greek subjects of the Sultau, nevertheless assures more than ever freedom of conscience at the same time that it destroys the supremacy which the Czars arrogated to themselves, the political object of which, the better to impose, was concealed under a religious mask. " As regards the third of those conditions þÿ that which has for object to limit the preponderance of Russia in the Black 8c a þÿ we have reserved it expressly as the most important arid most contested, so as to explain it here categorically. First of all, how must it be understood? Evidently anything equivocal on so grave a point cannot suit any one. 1 lie allied Governments, who have a consciousness of the justice of their pretensions, have not feared defining them. Russia has turned the Black Sea into a Russian lake ; she has gradually founded maritime establishments there of the first class; she has accumulated there, with as much perseverance as mystery, considerable naval forces, and it may be said that by that exclusive domination of the Black Sea she has placed Gonstantinople in a permanent state of siege.

' This state of things is not possible, because it is incompatible, not only with the integrity of the Ottoman empire, but with the security of the whole of Europe. " France and England, in demanding Russia to limit her power in the Black Sea, or to neutralize that sea, are therefore completely in their right. If that result was not obtained by peace or bv war, such a peace would be ephemeral and such a war useless ; an I, let it be well observed, this demand for the limitation ol Russian power, or for the neutralization ol the Black Sea, does not respond only to Anglo-French interests, it responds also to Hie interests of Austria, for which the Danube, a commercial and military river, is a magnificent highway, open to her activity towards the Euxine nnd Asia. An argument is brought against this pretension which we do not think serious; it is said to the Allied Powers You ask a concession from Russia, which at most might be the price of the surrender of Scbastopol, and that place is still held by the Russian army.' Our reply is this : þÿ ' The law ol nations grants that a portion of what is obtained by war may be kept by peace. We have not yet taken Sebastopol, that is true; but what is Subustopol nt the present moment to Russia? It is no longer a naval port ; ns her fleet, sunk at the mouth of the harbour, or shut up behind that insurpassablc barrier, is withdrawn front the struggle. The Black Sen is the battlefield which we have þÿwon or, if they like it which has been abandoned to us by the ene-

my. The Russian Hag could not show itself there. Our ships and those of England and Turkey navigate it in every sense. Its domination has changed hands. It has gone Irom Sebastopol to Constantinople.' " Who compels us to give up this pledge ? Is not such a situation the very best we could have? Sherman rose and very composedly remarked : þÿ "I shall not discuss politics with Mr. Smith before the court ; hut I am perfectly willing to argue questions of law, to chop logic, or even to split hairs with him." þÿ(31 The following Address and Reply have been sent to us for insertion: ADDRESS. To the Reverend P. J. þÿMc Guirk, Minister of the Roman Catholic Church, Christiansted, St. Croix, West Indies. Reverend Sir, On the eve of your departure from this Island, we the undersigned Inhabitants, of the different Denominations as well as Catholics in the Jurisdic-

tion of your Pastoral charge, with feelings of true sympathy for yourself and deep concern for your afflicted Congregation, beg to present to you, this Testimonial of our high approbation of your conduct, as a Minister and a Gentleman, for the short time of Two and a half Years, in which you have administered here. Your pious and enlightened discourses, your assiduous attention to your Ministerial Calling, visiting, comforting and assisting. the sick, the poor and the needy þÿ dispensing without partiality hypocrisy or to all alike, the means of saving grace, together with your gentlemanly bearing and manly conduct through good and evil report, have won for you the esteem and admiration of this community. We beg to condole with you iu your present sorrows, reminding you that the disciple cannot be above his master, neither the servant above his Lord, but it is enough for you, that like your Lord and Master, you have suffered persecution, as an evidence of your high calling in Christ. Hoping that the all-wise disposer of events may so order all things, that you may again return to us, we wish you all the peaceful happiness of this life aud the glorious reward of the life to come. We remain, Reverend Sir, With feelings of respect and esteem, Yours, faithfully, St. Croix, 21th May 1855. (Here follow 636 signatures. )

REPLY. My dear Friends and Brethren iu Christ ! Perhaps there is no event so trying in the life of a Missionary Priest as that when, after a few years of labor, after identifying himself with, and as far as health and human frailty would permit, watching over the spiritual welfare of his Flock, he is about to take his departure from them for I1CW duties This is my enso at this moment ; but it is in obedicucc to the call of our Bishop, whom Christ lias given to rule over this portion of His militant kingdom. We must eheerfuMy submit at all times ; because it is the þÿ Will of God made manifest to þÿus and His will is our sanctification ; the ways and means are his own. Your affection, my friends, has induced you to over-oulogisc my humble labours, during my short residence amongst you. 1 feel t hat 1 have done nothing but what was my duty to have done and what the Priest of God must always be prepared to do, even at the sacrifice of his life. However, now, that it is the will of God that I should be separated from you þÿ yen my good, my kind, my hospitable, my sincere and faithful Flock þÿ for this you arc with few, indeed, very few exceptions ; is it not consoling to me, does it not buoy me up, to know that I am leaving with the esteem, the good wishes and sympathy, not only of my own congregation, but also that of all persons of all denominations ? How I merit such 1 am really at a loss to know ! This, at all events, is the case as lias been publicly manifested, and this, nothing except death, shall ever

efface from my memory. My beloved congregation, it is needless to assure you that 1 shall never at the altar ol God offer up the adorable sacrifice without imploring the Divine Victim before me, by 1 1 is precious blood, to be merciful to you. Yes even to my enemies, for they will require it þÿ ciating tortures of remorse when the excru- that worm that never þÿdieth shall have commenced to prey upon their unfortunate souls. My dear friends, let me finally impress upon your minds that language fails, that words could give you no idea of my feelings of gratitude, suffice it to say, the vivid recollections of your kindness shall live in iny soul, and be enshrined in my heart to its very last pulsation. And when the measure of our earthly existence shall be filled up þÿ when the days of our mortality shall reach their limit, after having given to Caiser the things that are þÿCwser s, and to God the things that are þÿGod þÿ s may we meet never to be separated in that Heavenly Kingdom, where as children of Christ, we shall he rewarded with unfading Garlands of Victory and Crowns of Eternal Life. Farewell my Friends, farewell, and if we part to meet no more on earth, I trust we will meet in Heaven. P. J. þÿMc GUIRK St. Croix, Christiansted 28th May 1855

The þÿ þÿAVIS. (.'Krittumsted, Friday the \bth Junt 1 85?' This number being our final issue, we beg, for the last time, to offer a few remarks. In saying our final issue, vve hope we will not be misunderstood, and the proprietor be taken for the publisher. The establishment is yet the property of the same person, who, undisturbedly, holds the Royal þÿGovernment s license. During the period we have appeared before the public, from the 14th December 1851 to date, we have always endeavoured, even with those innumerable difficulties we have had to encounter, to give that satisfaction, which is so essentially necessary to establish the respectability of a newspaper. We must, however, confess that more and much more could have been done; but the want of pecuniary aid frustrated all our plans, and thus situated, often without paper to print the gazette, frequent strikes of our workmen for payment of their wages, and no resources, how could it be possible that we could maintain anything like a good position? No, no have perfectly assured, would one, we are done better; for with such burdens as those we have previously alluded to, every effort we made proved fruitless. If then anything rashly or unjustly has been said as to the worth and merit of the þÿ þÿAvis, it has certainly been done without reflection or consideration, I and perfectly at variance with reason and justice. Before we conclude we have one more duty to perform þÿ that is gratitude to all our benefactors. We perform that duty now, and return them our hearty thanks for the patronage
they have so generously bestowed upon, and we beg to assure them that we shall ever feel grateful.

The " AVIS." Christiansted , Tuesday the 19 th June 1856. Government having responded to our just demands for remuneration for public work, we have been induced to continue the publication of the Avis. We Cublish e sent to each Subscriber, trusting, that to-day a Proposal which will the inducement held out in the same, may enable us to obtain a sufficient number of subscribers. In another part of our paper we have inserted a list of those which we have at present. We contemplate, if the number of subscribers can be increased to 150, to reduce the price of subscription to $5; and if to OOO $ A. W« (met lliuru fo t a , (hot 1 1 © public will consider it their duty to come forward in supporting a public Press, which although of humble pretensions, has always been considered as indispensable; and the loss of which never can be considered less than a public reproach. We have assumed the editorship of this paper, in the discharge of the duties of which, we hope to give as much satisfaction as can reasonably be expected. In a community, like ours, where there may be said to exist no public spirit, it will be difficult to satisfy the thousand demands of so many different critics. One demands a paper exclusively confined to Politics; another thinks that something else may be inserted, since lie has already read all the Political News in the foreign papers, from which we have made our extracts. While a third looks for domestic news, when such a commodity does not exist. We are aware, at the threshold of our undertaking, of the difficulties of our

position. But we trust to be enabled to become "all things to all men" so that while we cannot at every issue please all our readers, we may still hope to please some. Our columns are open for the discussion of any question which circumstances may call forth. We will not blindly adhere to the opinions of any party. While we shall aid the public in the expression of their opinion on matters concerning the welfareof the community, we will also endeavour to assist the Government in disabusing the public mind of erroneous impressions, and afford a steady support to the cause of order. We are not for the Government nor for the people þÿ but for both. Our selections shall be made with as much care as time and circumstances will allow. We shall, as soon as possible make the necessary arrangements for the supply of some of the many interesting Journals of Europe and America ;

3 "J; nt ® it x. a?is provided we are enabled to meet this, not inconsiderable expense. We are obliged, however, to issue but a half sheet until we can obtain sufficient hands for the proper conduct of the business.

From the New York Herald, May 20. Interesting from Japan. TFRRIDLL EARTHQUAKE IN NIPnON-PAR T1CUL ARS OF THE LOSS OF THE RUS- SIAN FRIGATE HI AAA. We have already had intelligence of the great earthquake which occurred in the island of Niphon on the 23d of December, whereby the towns of Ohosaca and Simoda were destroyed, and Jeddo much injured, and the Russian frigate Diana lost. We find in the Courrier du Havre the following details of the latter event: þÿ As we have already informed our readers, an earthquake of the most violent kind has taken place at Japan and among other misfortunes has occasioned the loss of the Russian frigate Diana The American steamer Powhatan, which was in the same vicinity, and which saved many of the ship-wrecked mariners, has prepared an account of its voyage from Japan to Shanghae, from which the Novelist, of Marseilles, has borrowed some details on the shipwreck of this Russian vesel. The frigate which was lost in the midst of this shocking catastrophe had on board the Vice Admiral Putiatin, engaged at the time in completing the treaty between Russia and Japan. She was at anchor in the port of Simoda Froa: the moment of the first shock of earthquake the sea exhibited such a movement of eddying and whirling, that in less than thirty minutes the ship pirouetted round herself more than forty uuujqiiug tanvl IniOtiug till lllU CllttlUI llUlding her The motion was so rapid that no one on board could keep on his legs, and all were seized with vertigo When the sea retired, the frigate which drew twenty ono feet of water, was

left in eight feet of water only. On its return, the sea rose to the height of five fathoms above its ordinary level, and in again retiring it left the frigate in less than four feet of water, so that the auchor stocks were visible. The agitation of the bottom of thj sea was so great at the time, that the Diana, though only in four feet of water, was borne to a great distance The officers believed that the port was about to become the mouth of a submarine volcano ready to engulf them. When the frigate next found herself afloat it was perceived that she was filling, and that the keel and the rudder had been torn away, and were floating along side. By passing sails under the ship they succeeded in keeping her afloat ; and on the next day, the sea having become calm they brought the frigate into deeper water Some shocks were again felt, but they were not attended by any serious consequence. After having repaired damages as well as they could, and constructed a temporary rudder, the weather being fine again, they attempted to bring the frigate into a bay less exposed, nnd where they might more easily complete repairs. But when they were at a distance of seven miles from Simona, a tempest blew up. The Japanese boats, to the number of over a hundred, which were towing the Diana, abandoned her, after having, however, taken in all her officers and crew ; and shortly after the ship was swallowed up in the sea. It must be remarked, says the Novelist, that tho Diana, which was pursuing the Napoleon

III., was perfectly disposed to disregard the neutrality of the port where the latter ship was lying, and to capture her even in those neutral wators if she could. The French vessel, however thanks to the rapid manoeuvres of her cap-

tain, Lopez, had set sail and departed from Simoda twelve hours before the arrival of the Russian ship. The city of Simoda has been so overthrown, that hardly a trace of its streets is distinguishable. þÿ nrOOO® From the New York Tribune, May 18.

SLAVERY IV MARYLAND. At a late session of the Anne Arundel County Court in Maryland a lot of slaves manumitted by their owuer, who died in 1846 when they numbered 70, were remanded into Slavery by decree of the Court. The case was briefly as follows : John Townshend, an eccentric old farmer of Prince George's County in that State, who by his own exertions had become the possessor of seventy slaves and property beside to the amount of thirty or forty thousand dollars, died in the year 1846 and in his will gave freedom to all his slaves and bequeathed to them hi9 property. For many years previous to his decease he had declared his intention of doing this to his friends and neighbors, some of whom tried bard to dissuade him from his purpose. In addition to his will he executed before his death a deed of manumission in order to make sure if possible of the freedom of his slaves in case his heirs should succeed in breaking his will, an attempt which he seemed to foresee. The will was contested, as in all such cases it is sure to be, and a trial took place, but the will was sustained An appeal was taken to the Superior Court when that judgment was reversed, the will broken and the property given to the claimants. The late trial ;n Anne Arundel County was on the deed of manumission, which followed the fate of the will and was declared invalid and void, thus consigning the whole bodv of Deeroes back to that Slavery which a humane or conscience-stricken master had endeavored to secure for them

As is usual in all such cases the plea was that the testator and manumittor was not in his right mind If he had been he would not have doue so foolish a thing as free seventy slaves and furnish them the means to start on a life of Freedom under favorable circumstances. To be sure his purpose had been disclosed for many years previous to his death, and his will and deed of manumission did nothing more than realize this long-favored intention But all this went for nothing before the Court which had the ultimate adjudication of the case. Who will pretend to disbelieve that the C ourts in the slave States are particularly careful of the legal rights of the negro ?

From the lllustated London News, May 19. RESIGNATION OF GENERAL CANROBERT.

' General Canrobert, in consequence of ill health, has committed his command ofthearmyto General Pelissier; but, not willing to leave the seat of war, has placed himself at the head of General Pelissier's division. The Moniteur of yesterday announces that the Emperor has received the following þÿ robert : despatch from General Can- Crimea, May 1(5, Ten a. m. My shattered health no longer allowing me to continue in the chief command, my duty towards my Sovereign and my country compels me to ask you to transfer the command to General Pelissier, a skilful and experienced leader. The army which I leave him is intact, hardened to war, full of ardour and confidence. 1 beseech the Emperor to leave me a soldier's place ( place de combatant) as commander of a simple division. The Minister of War has addressed the following reply to General Canrobert : þÿ Paris, May 16, Eleven p. m. The Emperor accepts your resignation. He regrets that your health has suffered ; he congratulates you upon the sentiment which makes you ask to remain in the army, where you shall have the command, not of a division, but of the corps of General Pelissier. Hand over the chief command to that General.

Froni the Observer, May 27, 1 855. GENERALS CAN ROBERT \nd PEI.1S1ER " Look here upon this picture anil on this." Willi respect to General Canrohcrt, Ins retirement from the commaiid-in-cliief had become indispensable. His methodical and prudent character was not in harmony with the state of the army. The army had become impatient, and he possessed the contrary virtue, perhaps, to excess; it attributed every fault to its chief, and the general had become the object of its suspicion, and even of its dislike. Everything that went wrong was attributed to him ; he was blamed for what was done, and for what was left undone. His prudence was called weakness; he was accused of incapacity, if not worse ; he began to lose Ins authority, and his presence at the head of his army would have soon endangered its chance of success, and destroyed what yet remained of the spirit ot discipline. There was, perhaps, some exaggeration in all this ; hut, right or wrong, such was the feeling; and, what is still more strange, the unpopularity which attached to the Commander-in-Chief extended even to Generals Bosquet and Niel. General Bosquet had enjoyed an excellent reputation, and great things were expected of him. The feeling changed, and, as in su«h circumstances men are often unjust, they who censured him affected to find out that as a man of action even General Bosquet was deficient. The favourable opinion expressed hy General Niel of the conduct of the siege operations was one cause of his unpopularity; hut what principally mi-
litated against his reputation was, that the works at Sebastopol did not fall

down before him as at Bomarsund. That general is now said to be a mere engineer, well acquainted, no doubt, with the rules and resources of his art, but not sufficiently aware of all that the quality of the soldier can add to those resources, and that what is impossible with indifferent troops, is possible, and even easy of execution, with those whose impetuosity knows no obstacle. Be this as it may, neither of the three generals lias retained the authority he once possessed with the army. In the same degree that the French army was dissatisfied with its generalin-chief, it is proud and happy in its new commander, and his presence has revived its spirit and its confidence. He is endeared to them by his good qualities ; and even his defects are in accordance with tlie present disposition of the troops, and the passion which agitate them, If General Canrobert is liesitating or over-prudent, General Pelissier knows not what doubt or hesitation means ; he is intrepid, hold, and audacious. lie is of a character that brooks no delay, recoils at no obstacle ; the slowness of the siege does not suit his fiery temper; and it is a matter of indifference to him what men are lost in a coup de main, provided it succeeds. As lie is as regardless of his own life as that of others, and as he is always, by day and hy night, as foremost in clanger as a young sub-lieutenant who longs for "the cross of honour" and for promotion, no one thinks it extraordinary or deserving of blame that he is as reckless of others

as he is of his own person. These are the qualities which distinguish liirn, and make him popular. He is as great a favourite with the army as his predecessor was the contrary, and as it is, in point of fact, the army which removed General Canrobert, so it is the army which named General Pelissier. The Emperor could not more have given it any other chief than he could have continued General Canrobert in the command. General Pelissier has won the admiration of the men by his bravery, his intelligence, and determination. Whatever has been done hy the French worthy of notice si nee the days of Alma anil Inkerman, is due to him ; it is lie who lias ever taken the initiative, and who has acted sometimes in spite of the orders of General Canrobert. It was he who first conceived the idea of the night attack of the 2d against the approaches which the Russians had erected against the left of the French army. He communicated his plans of that attack to General Canrobert, who ended by approving them. Pelissier, in consequence, made his preparations. The attack was to commence at ten o'clock at night. At six o'clock an aide-de-camp came to Pelissier's quarters with orders from General Canrobert not to proceed with the operation for reply. " We begin our work in four the present. "It is too late," was the hours." He kept his word, and the result was not only glorious but useful. He took nine mortars from the Russians, which were already in battery, and the feat is without example in the campaign.

This coup filled the measure of General Canrohert's unpopularity; it placed Pelissier where he is, and we may now indeed confidently anticipate that the war will enter into a new phase. The new plan of campaign is said to be of General Pelissier's conception; and from the known character of that officer it is not too much to expect it will be something very daring, and more approaching what is termed the grand guerre than any we have as yet witnessed in the Crimea. It is not probable that his plan has been communicated to many, consequently any idea as to its nature must be vague. It is, however, surmised

that his intention is to make a bold attempt to cut off the Russian army from Sebastopol, drive it into the interior of the country, and, establishing himself or. the ground now occupied by them, to do what the Russians attempted to effect at Inkerman. But, whatever be the new plan of operations, it is certain that important events are considered imminent at the seat of war ; General Pelissier will assuredly not remain idle, and we may expect, from one day to another, to hear of something decisive having taken place. The irresolution of General Canrobcrt was the cause why the general assault, which was to have been made on Sebastopol on the 28th of last month, did not take place. It had been settled in a council of war that the grand attack should be made at one o'clock in the morning of the day in question, and the British were quietly getting underarms, when the French commander sent word to Lord Raglan that he had changed his mind. It is now known that General Canrohert was the cause why nothing was attempted at Kertch. Some steamers belonging to the allied fleet, with 14,000 or 15,000 men on board, had just entered the Straits of Kertch, when they saw a French steamer following them, and making signals for them not to continue their voyage. When the vessel came up her captain delivered instructions to the French admiral to relurn, General Camobert having received a telegraphic order from Paris to fetch the French reserves from the Bospliorus. An English steamer arrived soon

after with a message from Lord Raglan to Sir Edmund Lyons desiring him to proceed alone, if he thought there was any prospect of success. The gallant sailor knew that the garrison of Kertch consisted of 10,000 men, and was therefore obliged to return. It is considered very fortunate for the military reputation of France and England that General Canrobert has resigned his command.

DEFEAT OF THE RUSSIANS. Saturday. May 26. The Moniteur publishes two despatches from General Pelissier, dated the 23d and 24th inst. In the first the General thus expresses himself: þÿ "The enemy had formed between the Central Bastion and the sea a large place d amies , where they proposed assembling considerable forces to make important sorties against us. "In the night between the 22d and 23d we attacked those works, which were defended by nearly the whole of the garrison. The combat was lierce, and lasted during nearly the whole of the night. We carried and occupied half of the works. I hope to be able to announce to you to-morrow that the remainder will have been carried on the following night." In the other despatch, General Pelissier says þÿ We last night very happily carried the remainder of the works we had attacked on the previous evening. The whose losses were enormous the enemy, night before, did not make so stout a resistance. Our losses, though considerable, were much less. "The allied armies today cordially celebrated together the birth-dav of her Majesty"

POSTURE OF EVENTS IN THE CRIMEA. The circumstances under which we enter upon the more active period of this campaign are highly favourable. A new general, who is known to be an officer of great energy, enterprise, and resolution, takes the chief command of

a <© ut <Q u a T as the French army. The whole reserve of the French troops assembled at Maslak was reviewed by the Sultan on the 12th of May, and the embarkation of this magnificent army of picked troops (for such it may be called) commenced on the same day. On the 14th two divisions of infantry under General Aurell and General Herbillon put to sea ; and on the 16th they were followed by the division of the Imperial Guard, 7, DUO strong, under General Regnault de St. Jean d'Angely, and by the cavalry, including two regiments of Cuirassiers, reckoning nearly 1,000 sabres. These sealed from the Bosphorus with troops sailed orders, and their destination was not known at Constantinople, but it has since been ascertained that they proceeded at once to Kamiesch. According to the French statements, the arrival of this additional army of 30,000 men raises the effective force of our gallant allies in the Crimea to no less than 125, 000 men ; the Turkish army under Omar Pasha at Eupatoria amounts to upwards of 50,000; the British army has regained its strength oi 30.0J0 ; and the Sardinian Contingent adds 15,000 troops þÿ being, in all, a combined force of 220,000 men. Even assuming these returns to be somewhat exaggerated, it may be confidently asserted that the allied armies do not fall short of 200,000 men, and they consist, in great part, of the finest troops in Europe. A more powerful and intrepid army never took the field, and, if the ability of the commanders is at all equal to the strength and spirit of the men,

such a force ought to suffice to sweep the Russians in less than six weeks from the Crimea. In this extraordinary war the expectations most reasonably and confidently entertained have been too frequently deceived either by inevitable accidents, by unaccountable oversights, or by the evils inseparable from a divided command ; but we should feel surprise amounting to astonishment if armies like those which General Pelissier and Lord Raglan have under their command do not speedily and triumphantly accomplish great and decisive results. Those armies are now of four times the strength of that gallant host which landed at Old Fort last September, and drove the Russians from the heights of Alma in three hours. The men are far more inured to the fatigues of war than they then were ; the officers better acquainted with the theatre of war, with the enemy, and with their own duties. Eupatoria and Balaklava, which may be considered as tbc extreme left and right of our position, are connected by an easy steam navigation of four hours. The whole coast between these two points is at our command. There is safe anchorage for the fleet and transports along the whole shore, a beach admirably adapted for landing, streams of water running down from the interior at short distances, and an open country highly favourable to the evolutions of an army. It is said, and probably with truth, that Omar Pasha has declared that he would undertake to advance upon and occupy Simpheropol with his own troops, supported

by the French army of reserve under General Regnault de >St. Jean d'Angely, and we cannot entertain a doubt that such an operation is perfectly feasible, even without any material diminution of the forces hitherto engaged in the defence of our lines of countervallation and in the works of the siege.

THE EARL OF DUNDONALD'S PLAN FOR TAKING SEBASTOPOL IN A DAY. Sir, þÿ Peace being desirable, not only for the interests of our countrys but for those of the world at large, and the negociations now pending heing doubtless injuriously influenced by the ob-

stinate resistance of Sebastopol, (which could be overcome in a day), and by the imposibility of successfully attacking Cronstadt by naval means (which might be as speedily reduced,) I have drawn up a petition to Parliament, iu order that secrecy and silence on my part, and deficiency of information on that of the public, may no longer prove injurious to the success of our arms Hostilities having proceeded so far, assuredly it is most expedient to reduce a restless nation to a third or fourth rate Power than be ourselves reduced. Let not my motive be mistaken. I have no wish to command a fleet of 100 gun ships, or to attack first-rate fortresses by encased batteries or steam gun-boats ; that which I desire is, first, secretly, to demonstrate to competent persons tbc efficiency of my plans and then to obtain authority (during eight or ten days of fine weather) to put them in execution The means I contem plate are simple, cheap, and safe in þÿexecution they would spare thousands of lives, millions of money, and great havoc and uncertainty of results. Their consequences might, and probably would effect the emancipation of Poland, and givo freedom to the usurped territories of Sweden My unsupported opinion in regard to a naval enterprise in 1809 proved to be correct and every other undertaking in the British service, uid as Commander-in-Chief in Chili, Peru, Brazil, and Greece was successful, and so would the protracted and unaccomplished undertakings (so injurious to the result of negotiation have succeed-

From the lllustated London News, May 19. TROUBLES IN RUSSIA. The most important intelligence from St. Petersburg is the alleged resignation of Count Nesselrode þÿ caused, it is said, by his opposition to the war party in the Russian Cabinet. The cautious old Chancellor has, no doubt, good reason to argue in favour of accepting such terms as the Allies have offered. The recent accounts from the Ukraine represent the insurrectionary spirit among the peasantry as very far from being suppressed. In other parts of Russia the heavy requisitions are causing loud complaints, nor is it at all unlikely that the Government may find work enough for a large portion of its army at home, if the disaffection should spread, as is highly probable. In Poland, on the other hand, where the oppressive system has been carried out most rigorously, the Government has all at once adopted the mild method. Letters from Warsaw affirm that measures calculated to give just satisfaction to Poland are impatiently expected there, and that the police has been extremely indulgent ; so much so, that people talk freely of public matters at cafes and theatres þÿ a tiling unheard of before, and which excites the astonishment of all those who know what severity there was before. This, however, may be only a ruse of the authorities for the purpose of ascertaining what the real opinions of the people are, with a view to check any free movement in concert with the Allies.

In answer to a question relating to the mysterious engine proposed by Lord Dundonald to beemployed in the destruction of Sebastopol and Cronstadt, Lord Palmerston has said that, although he could say nothing positive, it appeared to him that the difficulties of its employment were almost unconquerable. One cannot guess what may be the exact nature of Lord Dundonald's invention ; but no very deep science is requisite to know that there exist explosive mixtures compared with which gunpowder is as harmless as a child's toy, and which, introduced, even in small quantities, within a hostile fortress, would by their explosion absolutely pulverise the most solid ramparts. Probably the most active agent of this kind with which we arc acquainted is that which chemists call chloride of azote (a combination of chlorine gas and nitrogen) which has hitherto been only procured in the form of very small globules, of an oily liquid. The explosive force of this substance far exceeds that of any other known. Almost anything þÿ even a bare touch by a piece of metal þÿ sets it off ; and a globule no bigger than a large pea will blow a hole in a thick table. A pint bottle of this agreeable fluid would certainly blow Sebastopol "into the middle of next week," if a man in a balloon could drop it into one of the batteries. It is onlv a question if it would not also

blow the Allied armies and the Crimea itself into the BlackSea. But then who could, or would, make a pint bottle of it ? þÿ or, supposing it made, and the city containing the manufacturer's laboratory to have escaped the dangers of the process, who is to take charge of it, or carry it where it is wanted Y Many people think that Lord Dundonald's plan lias some reference to the use of balloons. If so it would not be the first time that balloons have been used in warfare : they were successfully employed by Dumouriez for the purpose of reconnoitring, 1 think, before the battle of Jemappes þÿ Ibid, May 20.

A paper published in Stettin contains a letter from the captain of a Hanoverian vessel, (who, during the war between Germany and Denmark in 1848-9 had made a feigned sale of his vessel to a Russian, as a protection against the Danes,) in which he warns all his countrymen who may have resorted to the same artifice, not to visit the port of London during the present war, inasmuch as there are persons there well acquainted with the German coasting shipping, who for the sake of the reward offered to those who denounce enemy's property in England are ready and willing to put the owners of vessels so situate to great expense and loss by denouncing their craft, although wrongfully, as Russian property. þÿ London Times, May 8.

The British and French envoys have received instructions to communicate to the Danish Cabinet that their Governments can no longer acknowledge the neutrality of Denmark, but insist in the most serious manner on her declaring openly as a friend or a foe. A similar demand has been made on the Swedish Government. þÿ IVillmer <y Smith's Times.

A private letter from Brussels says, þÿ The King of Sweden has positively refused to take an active part in the war against Russia. He alleges the want of sufficient guarantees as the reason against his rushing into a war of conquest and aggrandizement. For Sweden to give her co-operation would be it necessary for England and France to bind themselves by a treaty of 10 years, at least to leave at her disposal a force always ready to repel every attack on the part of Russia. þÿ Times, June 2.

From our own Correspondent, Southampton, June 2, 1855. Dear Sir þÿ By the Royal Mail Company's Steamship Tay, Captain Moir, I forward you my usual news-letter which contains some important intelligence respecting the progress of the war, which has for so long a period been so unsatisfactorily pending between Eastern and Western Europe. The scene of operations to which the attention of the Allied Powers has been directed, is the Sea of Azoff, which waters have fallen into the hands of the Allies almost without a casualty. Tho expedition which left about a fortnight since, landed its troops at Kerteh on Queen Victoria's birthday, and the enemy fled, blowing up their fortifications on both sides the Straits and destroying their steamers. On the 25th May, Sir George Brown destroyed a foundry near Kertch, where shot, shell, and Minie balls were manufactured. The Russians burned three of their steamers, trading and transport. As many more were captured In the evening the Allies entered the Sea of Azoff The Russians burned their magazines at Kerteh which contained 160,000 sacks ot oats, 360,000 sacks of corn, and 100,000 sacks of flour þÿ in all, 620,000 sacks of grain and flour intended no doubt for the use of the Russian forces in Sebastopol and tho neighbourhood. The "AVIS." Christiansted, Friday the 6th April 1s55. His Excellency Governor Feddersen returned to this Island on Tuesday evening last, from St. Thomas. The European Mails arrived here on W ednesday. The papers confirm 'the news of the death of the Emperor ot Russia, who died on the 1st March at St. Petersburg, in the 59th year of his age and the 30th of his reign. He is succeeded by his eldest son Alexander, born in 1818, and consequently in his 37th year. In the night between the 16th and 17th February the Russians, under General Osten-Sacken, attacked Eupatoria ; but were repulsed by the Turks under Omar Pasha, after a desperate conflict which lasted five hours. The loss of the Russians is estimated at 400 killed and 700 wounded. That of the Turks, at 87 killed and 277 wounded. Selim Pasha, Lieutenant General commanding the Egyptian troops, among the dead, and Sulei- is man Pasha among the wounded. Thirteen inhabitants of the town of Eupatoria lost their lives, and 11 were wounded. The French garrison of 200 men had four killed and eight wounded. The Russians, it is said, on their retreat from Eupatoria, set fire to the villages in which they had established themselves. The English menof-war Curacoa, Furious, Valorous and faer, and Viper, the the Turkish French Steamer Steamer Scheh- Volace, all contributed towards frustrating the efforts of the Russians. The death of the Grand Duke Michael, brother of the new Czar, is announced as having taken place before Sebastopol.
