The military and maritime authorities ot Corsica report the total loss of the French Frigate Semillant, and the lives of all on board þÿ 100 infantry besides her crew.

The announcement of the accession of Alexander II., was received with general satisfaction throughout England as the harbinger of a pacific policy, but the hopes however soon gave way to a less confident feeling. The Western Powers, therefore, at once wisely determined not to trust to the chapter of accidents, and the moment the intelligence of the death of the Czar was received by the Emperor of the French, orders were issued for prosecuting the siege of Sebastopol with increased vigour, and Lord Clarendon crossed over to Boulogne the same day and had an interview with his Majesty. Lord John Russell has reached Vienna, and although it had been presumed in some quarters that negotiations for peaee were progressing favourably, yet nothing which could be deemed authentic had transpired. The fact, however, that the Emperor of the French having declined his intended visit to the Crimea is pretty certain. The Independence Belye states that a new French corps d? nrmee is to be formed, composed of the troops now stationed near Boulogne. It will be styled the Army of the North, and Marshal Baraguay d'Hilliers will have the command. It is imagined by some that the sudden death of the Emperor of Russia may be followed by a proposal for an armistice by the enemy, which will scarcely be entertained.
From the Observer, March 11, 1855. THE LATE EMPEROR OF RUSSIA.

HIS LIFE AND REIGN. His reign has lasted 29 years, three months, and one day. The Emperor Nicholas has not died suddenly; he had been ill for 12 days before. We have before us letters from St. Petersburg of the 19th ult., which state that the Emperor then kept his bed by order of his first physician, Dr. Mandt. The Empress was also ill, and confined to her bed, and, as the apartments occupied by the Emperor and Empress are situated one on the ground floor and the other on the first floor of the palace, they had no direct communication, and did not see each other. The Emperor, however, must have called the Empress to him, as we know, from a telegraphic despatch, that before his death he had assembled round him all the members of his family present at St. Petersburg, in order to give them his blessing. Our correspondents attribute the illness of the Emperor to a cold. Notwithstanding the severity of the weather, he continued his usual occupations ; he was desirous to see everything for himself, and in the most minute details; he visited the soldiers in their barracks; he passed long and frequent reviews, forgetting the precautions which his age required in such a climate and in such a severe season. To all the observations made to him by his children and by his most devoted

servants, he replied that he had something else to do besides taking care of his health, lie had, however, attend ed to it for more than a year past, and at times felt some uneasiness. He said that he had reached, and even xceeded, the number of years which God had allowed to others of his race, and that his end was not far distant, fie had treated himself according to his own ideas; he had insisted on his physician putting hitn on a regimen which would prevent his getting corpulent, of which he had a singular dread. What change has taken place since the 19th of February? It is said that he had an attack of apoplexy, or a paralysis of the lungs. That was a thing which Dr. Mandt had not anticipated, for at that time he felt no alarm, and his language was most satisfactory. The Emperor Nicholas was, moreover, subject to attacks of gout, and at the commencement of his illness he had felt some symptoms of it. The new Sovereign of Russia was initiated at an early age into the affairs of the empire by the Emperor, his father; he was present at all the councils ; he was invested with situations which gave him frequent opportunities of rendering himself useful to the army and pleasing to the youth of the schools. Whenever the Emperor Nicholas quitted the capital he left the supreme direction of the government to his son, and, in short, he had taken the utmost pains to prepare him to become his successor. The Grand Duke Alexander, the heir to the Crown, is very popular in Russia ; he is beloved and

esteemed by the people He will not exercise the great authority of his father, for he does not inherit either his hauteur or his inflexibility. He will rather please as the Emperor Alexander the First did, by his mildness and his affability, and between the uncle and the nephew there is every great similarity of character in numerous ways. The new empress is also highly spoken of, and her elevated judgment and her conciliating manners are much extolled It is thought that she will exercise a salutary influence over the Emperor. Public opinion in Russia attributes to the hereditary Grand Duke a policy different from that of the Emperor, and particular a more pacific one. It is affirmed, either correctly or otherwise, that the Prince has not always approved the conduct followed for the last two years by the Cabinet of St. Petersburg in the Eastern question, and that he regretted the mission of Prince Menschikoff to Constantinople, and the invasion of the Principalities. It is impossible to foresee even the immediate consequences of the death of the Ehiperor Nicholas, but we think that the event will augment the chances of the re-establishment of peace. The Emperor Nicholas was in himself an obstacle to peace. He had been reproached with excess of his ambition and with the means which is sometimes employed to satisfy it. Notwithstanding his protestations, all the responsibility of the war was thrown on him, and he felt the deepest resentment at it. The st uggle, therefore, became in a measure one per-

sonal to him, and that obstacle to peace has now disappeared. It may, therefore, be hoped that the relations of the adversaries of Russia with her new Sovereign will be more easy than they were with the Emperor Nicholas, and that the conferences of Vienna will open under auspices favourable to the re-estabhshment of peace.

On the departure of the courier a heavy cannonade was going on. The batteries and trenches are completed. The order to attack is expected. Sebastopol, Feb. 24. þÿ Generals Bosquet and Campbell have reconnoitred the heights of Balaklava, and exchanged shots With the advanced posts of the Russians, who retired to the Tchernaya precipitately. still Sickness prevailed among the troops, but their morale was excellent. The siege operations were advancing. The fire was slack on both sides. The Russians were continually throwing up new fortifications. The railway was progressing. Advices from Kamiesch Bay, of the 24th of February, state that on the previous day the French had destroyed the works round the Malakhoff Tower, but with great loss. This is evidently the same attack as that mentioned in Prince Menschikoff's despatch below. Advices from Smyrna of the 25th of February state that 1,000 English sick had arrived at the hospital. A FURIOUS CANNONADE. Feb. 24. þÿ Shortly after two o'clock this morning commenced one of the most furious cannonades we have heard since the siege began. The whole line of the Russian batteries from our left opened with inconceivable force and noise, and the Inkerman batteries began playing on our right; but the French were most exposed to the weight of this most terrible fire, which shook the very earth, and lighted up the skies with incessant lightning Hashes for an hour and a half. Under cover of it a very strong sortie has been made, and for half an hour the musketry rolled incessantly with volume and vigour enough for a general action. Judging from the weight and extent of the fire the Russians must have been in large þÿbodies perhaps a sortie of 2,500 or 3,000 men, and as they were splendidly covered by the fire of their batteries, I do not think they could have suffered much when they were finally repulsed. The cannonade lasted from 2-15 a. 111. to 3-50 a. 111. In much of the time they fired, as I counted, 15 guns in 30 seconds, and sometimes the reports came in regular salvoes, and the flashes leaped forth in great flames to of tell so that it was impossible solid fire, what number of guns the enemy were working. The echoes of the reports towards the close among the hills in the distance increased the tumult.

RUSSIAN P R E P A RATIONS. Since the intention of the Western Powers to land an army in Finland has been known at St. Petersburg, the Russian Government directs its most serious attention to that quarter. The last accounts received from Finland, via Sweden, announce that the military chiefs display the greatest activity in placing in a state of defence all the points along the coast of the two gulfs where landings might be effected. The inhabitants, on their side, exhibit the utmost emula tion, and afford every assistance in thenpower to the officers of engineers charged with the erection of these works of defence. The formation of twenty Finnish battalions, decreed in November by the Emperor, is proceeding rapidly. Their armament was supplied by the arsenals of Sweaborg and Helsingforts ; hut the districts dress and equip their respective contingents at their own expense. In anticipation of important military events, the Government has ordered the establishment in the interior, within a few leagues of the coast, of hrispitals and lazarettos, for the soldiers and seamen of the gunboat flotillas.

The Knout. þÿ This instrument of tor ture, which unhappily is unknown out of the Muscovite empire, inflicts so dreadful a chastisement, that a single blow when struck upon particular parts of the back or side, is sufficient to deprive a human being of life. I have often been assured that if the criminal be rich enough, he pays the wretch destined to be his executioner, to put him as speedily as possible out of his pain, by striking him in a vital part. The executioner, it is said, is always made intoxicated before hand. A university student, who had, after being treated with great injustice by the professor, struck him in a moment of anger, was tried, and sentenced by the Emperor himself, to receive a thousand lashes. When the day arrived on which the unfortunate young man was to suffer for his imprudence, the whole of the students and professors were ordered to be assembled to witness his punishment, the horrible details of which can scarcely be conceived. At every blow of the barbarous knout, a long line of flesh flew out, until the bones were quite bare and the heart was exposed to view. Of course, long ere this, the unfortunate victim had ceased to breathe, but the sentence was a thousand lashes, and whether he was alive or dead, the number must be given. Several of the horror-stricken students, the spectators of this disgraceful sight, were lying insensible on the ground, having fainted with dismay, and my informant shuddered as he mentioned that a piece of flesh fell

on his own sleeve as the knout was uplifted, At St. Petersburgh, lines of carriages, filled with ladies (to their shame afid disgrace) are drawn up in a line as spectators of this diabolical execution, and one amiable countess gave a feeling and animated description of the horrid scene at an evening party.

Notice. The undersigned Vestry lor St. Paul s Church Fredericksted have received notice from the Rec.tor of his intention to resign the charge of said Parish on the 1st of June next. From the West Indian, March 9. BARBADOS. Agricultural Review. But little progress was made in reaping the Crop during the last month, the canes not being ripe enough, and the wind slack. There were two days of rain in the beginning, and two at the close of the month; and the fall of rain for the month in this Parish, 3 inches, which is more than usual. In St. Tho-

more frequent. The weather has been remarkably cool. It has an excellent effect upon the ripening canes, and the young crop, which everywhere is regular and vigorous. Seldom have we enjoyed a more favorable planting season ; soaking rains from time to time, ever since the I st of January, yet not so heavy as to remain on the ground and drown the plants, and frequent showers. They have been not less beneficial to the old

turity. The reaping is delayed in conwhere prevailed. The safety of the em- ! sequence, but that is no great evil, and it is counterbalanced by the larger yield and better quality of the canes. What sugar has been made is of a fair quality. i The quantity shipped up to the end of this month was 912 hhds. The weather has been favorable for the planting of Provisions, which are more abundant than usual at this season. As soon as the canes are cut, the field is put into potatoes, which is the only thing they plant just now in the way of provisions,

except it may be bonavist. So that we are likely to have potatoes in abundance in May and June þÿ a great thing for the laborer and the poor. The highest readings of the Barometer was on Sunday the 4th, which reached as high as 30: 10, and the lowest on Thursday 22d, giving a mean of 29: 99. The temperature ot the Fahrenheit Thermometer presents much uniformity, and gives an average for the whole month of 80 degrees. The wind has been steady to the East and North East, save calms at times, and two days, 20th and 21 st, it goes far to the North West þÿ an unusual event at this season of the year. The coldest night for the month, and indeed as yet lor the year, was on the night of the 21st, and fell as low as 63 degrees, by the self registering Thermometer. On Tuesday the 13th, and Saturday the 24th, we were blessed with two deep seasons of Rain, to the extent of over an inch each day, and the aggregate for the month was three inches. Upon the whole, we have enjoyed at this elevation a comfortable and delightful month. B. T. YOUNG. Grand View, March J.

A London paper says : " How often is the old saw verified, that necessity is the mother of invention.' We are at war with Russia, and already two discoveries have been made and patented by which substitutes are provided, to a very considerable extent, for two of the chief articles we have hitherto imported from the realms of the Czar. The new system of grinding wheat by conical mills, it was stated by Sir John Shelly and Mr. C. Hindly, M. P., to Sir James Graham, that the Admiralty, would, if universally adopted in this country, save per annum as much flour, from the quantity used at present, as would feed one million more people. A patent has been taken out in the United Kingdom, France, Belgium, &c., for the making of soap by means of tallow extracted from materials hitherto considered nearly worthless, and which can be obtained at less than one-sixth the price paid for Russian tallow, and soap manufactured at a cost of £10 or £12 per ton cheaper than it has hitherto been. It possesses moreover, far more of the cleansing property than ordinary soap, and promises to be a great boon to laundresses on the one side, and cloth manufacturers especially on the other."

steamer El Dirado by :i S|> inisli frigite was based 11 >' > it unofficial intelligence, but so well iiuilieiilie.aled that we felt sin i litrias«'(l to rely upon its correctness. We have been favored by the Stale Department with a copy of a letter of Captain Gray, the commander of the El Dorado, addressed to the acting American Consul at Havana, which we publish below, and which fully sustains the account on which our comments of yesterday were made. The insult to our flijr was flagrant, wholly unprovoked, and without the shadow ol palliation. An armed Spanish man-of-war deliberately tires two shots at one of our regular mail steamers, stops her on her voyage by force, and compels her to submit to a search by a Spanish official. It is difficult to conceive of a grosser outrage upon our national fl ig, or a more deliberate insult to our national honor, or n holder assertion of " the right of search." If the case takes the usual course, the facts will he forwarded to Madrid, where the Spanish government will he called upon for reparation. The Span'sli government will claim lime to send to Havana to procure evidence; and in the meantime, whilst this delay takes place, -ome other American vessel will lie fired into and searched by another Spanish frigate, and in this way the insult mid injury are never acknowledged or atoned for. VVe will not pursue the subject, hut only remark that our flag and our honor have been instilled, and the r i irh t of search practically asserted. We have

full confidence that the President will do his duty faithfully in the premises. The letter of Captain Gray is as follows : þÿ Steamship El Dorado, ) Havana, March 8, 1855. ) Sir, þÿ I have to report to you that on the night of the 6th inst., while on my passage front Aspiiuvall (IV G ) towards this place, with the Unite. I Slates mails and California passengers, I was fired at, and brought to, by i lie Spanish frigate Ferolona, the circumstances of which are these : þÿ The night was beautifully clear, with a smooth sea ami light breezes from the south and east. At twenty minutes past midnight I made Cape Antonio light, hearing north by west, (per compass,) steering north by west | west, and a few minutes afterwards a ship was seen on our port how with Iter head to south and west and courses hauled up. At about I. 15. when she was two points forward of the beam, and distant front half to three-quarters of a mile, without signal of any description. she fired a shot at us, which fell about twenty yards from the ship on port side, abreast of fore rigging. I immediately ordered the helm put a starboard, and ran down towards her, intending to pass under her stern ; hut, when within three hundred yards of her, she fired a second shot, which passed «. but a short distance over the port wheelhouse from forward to aft. The engines having been previously slowed, I stopped them, and ranging up under Iter stern, nsked what lie wished. He rep'ied bv asking what ship it was. and

where I was froin. I told him the United States mail steam-ship ' El Dorado," from Aspinwall, hound to Havana, lie then told me to hack and wait. After stopping some minutes I again hailed and asked him what he wanted, and to know if he was go:ng to keep me there all night, lie answered by saying he would send a boat alongside, which lie did. When the officer came on hoard, lie requested to see the papers. I shewed him the clearance from the United States consulate at Aspinwall, ami also the bill of health; after reading which,

The detention of stopping being about 45 minutes, besides running out of my course I Would further remark that during the whole night niv signal lights were burning bright and clear and that I was pursuing in y course at a distance of fully eight or ten miles from any land, ami without the intention of violating the laws of any country. I remain, with respect, your obedient servant. A I. PR ED (J GRAY. W. II. Robertson, Esq., United States Consul. We, William Brown, second mate, and Joshua II. Walcott, passenger, of the steamer ! From Liberia. The Boston Traveller, April 24, gives the following summary of the latest news from the Republic of Liberia. The Liberia Herald, of Jan. 17th, contains the þÿPresident sAddress to the Senate and House ot Representatives of Liberia, detailing the result of his recent mission to Europe. The President went abroad for rest and recreation chiefly, but from his account, the six weeks which he spent in England and in France must have been weeks of constant, engrossing labor. His first care j seems to have been to disabuse the public mind of sundry prejudices against Liberia, in consequence of its connection with Colonization ; or rather, in consequence of the expressed opinions of certain Southern friends of Colonization. He so far succeeded in this, as to have the pleasure of hearing Joseph Sturgc, the Quaker, express in a large public meeting, that whatever might have been the motives of Southern advocates ot Colonization, Liberia seemed to be the child of heaven, and under the fostering care of Divine Providence, destined to do more for the elevation of the race, and towards the introduction of civilization and Christianity into Africa, than any other enterprise, civil or religious, hitherto conccived. Another object of attention was the plan of procuring a suitable port for naval purposes, such as repairs and construction, at Sierra Leone, for the benefit of Western Africa The proposition met with favor, and hopes are entertained that the Government of Great Britain may give

attention to the matter. From London, President Roberts went to and also to secure the promised uniforms Paris, to adjust some difficulties about the for treaty, the Liberia militia. He obtained the assurance that 1000 new uniforms should be manufactured for the Liberians, and forwarded, as a present, from the Emperor. He also obtained encouragement that a small vessel of war should be added as a further testimonial of the French þÿEmperor favor s towards the African Republic- Steps were also taken by the President to secure the recognition of Liberian independence by Saxony, Oldenburg, and the Hans Towns. In London, President Roberts met with several American gentlemen who expressed an anxious solioitiulo that the United States Government should acknowledge the independence of Liberia. The President also attended to sundry commissions for purchasing articles lor the use ol the Republic, among others a lighthouse and lamp for Cape Montserrado. He procured plates for paper bills of fifty cents up to five dollars ; and through the generosity of Mr. Gurney, coin had dies cut, and a quantity of copper ol London, struck for the Republic. He received £110 worth of Bibles and Testaments for distribution among the schools of Liberia from Sir H. St. Paul. The lhrald states that according to a recent decision of the Supreme Court of Liberia, the constitutional right of suffrage is confined to persons holding real estate. The Legislature of the Republic, at its of late session, passed a law for the suppression a the use of all intoxicating drinks. It imposes duty

of one dollar a gallon upon all spirituous and malt liquors. The dwelling house of the Rev. Alexander Crumwell, at Monrovia, was destroyed by fire on the 9th of January, lie sustained a severe loss. His card of thanks, published in the Herald, is worthy of notice. He returns heartfelt thanks to the þÿ Johnson þÿGuards, to the Gentlemen of the Four Council, and to the Wardens, Vestry, and active sympathising members of his congregation,

Atlt S both male and female, for their kindness and la- i bors. Of the young men, he cays ; þÿ Never have we witnessed more noble daring, more real hero- j ism, more generous enthusiasm. They are made of the stuff, which, if rightly used, will make them patriots for their country, and heroes for þÿChrist. Rev. John Kiugdon, missionary under the auspices of the Southern Baptist Convention of Fo- of reign Missions died at Monrovia on the 16th January. The Herald states that Hon, John M. Lewis, having resigned his editorial connection with that . paper, his place will be filled by Edward W country Blyden. Mr. Blyden came from Jamaica of a few years ago, for the purpose to this obtaining an education, and was advised to he go has Liberia, which he did, where it seems to found the means of education at least sufficient to qualify him for conducting the public press.

Mr. Blyden is a native of St. Thomas, and not of Jamaica as above stated, through the instrumentality of the Rev. J. P. Knox, late Reformed Dutch Minister in this Island, Mr. B was induced to proceed to the United States, where for a time lie received additional instruction to his previous attainments, and lastly recommended to complete his studies in the þÿ Alexander High þÿSchool, Monrovia. Doubtless the friends and acquaintances ot Mr. Bi.yden will be happy to peruse the foregoing - - Editor Tidende.

Make known : On the report of Our Minister of Finance, who has laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council in Our West-India Possessions on a Draft of Ordinance, concerning Taxes in the Island of St. Thomas to the Land-Treasury, We most graciously decree: þÿ I. The Store-tax to the Land Treasury of St. Thomas shall hereafter be levied on every public Store or Shop in the town, whether business there is carried on by Burgherbrief or by License, or the articles for sale are productions of handicraft. From the 1st of August 1854 the contributors of the Store Tax are to be divided into eleven classes, paying respectively #300, $225, $150, $100, $60, $40, $30, $20, $16, $12 and $6 annually, based on the extent of business carried on by the parties concerned. 2. The Tax of 4 per Cent of Rent, which has hitherto only been levied on properties, the buildings of which were subject to the rules laid down in the Ordinance of the 1st of October 1802 3, shall in future also be paid for vacant lots in town, as well as for those be yond the same, not belonging to Estates. 3. Instead of the present Lamp-tax, and in order to enable the Land-Treasury to defray the heavier expenses, connected with the repairs &c. of those principal streets, that are publicly lighted at present, or to which lighting may in future be extended, shall be paid : One eighth of the tax of 4 per Cent of the rent of all houses and lots in the above mentioned streets, to be collected together with said tax first time for the

year 1854. One fourth of the Store-tax of all public stores or shops in the same streets, to be collected together with the Store-tax from the 1st of August 1854. 4. For each horse in St. Thomas shall be paid an annual tax, as follows : a, for a horse kept in town, $4, h, for a horse kept in the country, $1£. 5. For carriages in town not exclusively intended for transport of goods, an annual tax shall be paid as follows : a, for a four-wheeled carriage, $12, h, for a two-wheeled ditto, $ 8. From this rule however, such carriages are exempted, that notoriously have not been in use for ihe last 6 months previous to the time the Tax is due.

6. For each vessel belonging to the Island of St. Thomas, and which is not of a tonnage making it liable to take out Sea-pass, an annual tax shall lie paid as follows: a, for a deck or half-deck boat with or without a small boat (yawl), $4, b, for a sail boat without deck, $2, c, for a row-boat, $1, d, for a boat kept to supply ships with water, $10, e, for a launch or lighter or other similar vessel, used for the transportation of merchandize in the harbour, 10 dollars. $ 7. From the Observer, May 13, 1855. ATTEMPTED ASSASSINATION OF THE EMPEROR OF THE FRENCH.

Pianori (otherwise Liverani), accused of attempting to assassinate the French Emperor, was tried on Monday before the Cour þÿd Assise of the Seine. The following is a translation of the indictment (acte d' accusation) against Pianori: þÿ þÿ Giovanni Piauori, who has procured a passport in the name of Liverani, was born in one of the Roman provinces, but which in particular he refuses to disclose. He is a bachelor, and a shoemaker by trade. Iu 1849, according to his own admission, he (as a volunteer soldier, as he styles himself ) formed part of the Roman insurrectional army under the orders of one of the revolutionary chiefs who then commanded it, hut who, he alleges, was unknown to him. About this time he was obliged to leave the Roman States, and he, with several others, took refuge in Piedmont, where he remained several years, and up to tho end of 1853 or the beginning of 1854. He afterwards went to Marseilles, where he stayod some months, under the name of Liverani, working at his trade for sailors þÿ at least so he says. Subsequently he is found running through various towns in France, Lyons, Cha- I leaves London, and comes again Ions, and then in Paris, where he took out a þÿ permit of þÿresidence in the name of Liverani. It does not appear that he had any very certain means of subsistence by his labour, He had an introduction to a master shoemaker in Paris, named Mallet, who agreed to give him work. After a sojourn of some months in Paris he suddenly started for London, where he says he j forced to admit the fact. During

stayed nearly three months. What was his motive for leaving France ? He lias not stated any ; out it miij tie amrmea with certainty that it was not for want of work that lie went to another country, since he never turned to good , sued forth from his lodgings armed to the teeth ; account the work that was offered him in Paris. However this may be, he arrived in London in the month of December, 1854, and there all at once he found means to earn 50s. a week (that is to say, nearly 55f). Such is his declaration ; but he says he cannot possibly tell who it was that employed him at these wages, nor the address of his employer, nor even in what part of the town he lived. Pianori then, according to his own statement, earned 5of. a week, and he further says that he put by, out of that sum, as much as 30f. a week. Now, since he had passed three months in London, he may, if he speaks tho truth, have saved as much as 300f. This is impossible, or at least improbable. No journeyman shoemaker can earn so much in London, and save so much after paying all expenses. Suddenly, instead of keeping a place where he was so exceedingly well off, he left London on March 26, and returned to Paris. What has he been doing since that period ? M. WE FREDERIK the SEVENTH By the grace of God King of Denmark, the Vandels and the Goths, Duke of Slelswick, Holsteen, Stormarn, Ditmarsh, Lauenborg and Oldenborg, Make known : On the report of Our Minister of Finance, who has laid before Us the deliberation of the Colonial Council in Our West-India Possessions on a Draft of Ordinance, concerning Taxes in the Island of St. Thomas to the Land-Treasury, We most graciously decree; þÿ I. The Store-tax to the Land Treasury of St. Thomas shall hereafter lie levied on every public Store or Shop in the town, whether business there is carried on by Burgherbrief or by License, or the articles for sale are productions of handicraft. From the 1st of August 1854 the contributors of the Store Tax are to be divided into eleven classes, paying respectively $300, $225, $ 150, $100, $60, $40, $30, $20, $10, $12 anil $6 annually, based on the extent of business carried on by the parties concerned. $ 2. The Tax of 4 per Cent of Rent, which has hitherto only been levied on properties, the buildings of which were subject to the rules laid down in the Ordinance of the 1st of October 1802 3, shall in future also he paid for vacant lots in town, as well as for those beyond the same, not belonging to Estates. 3. Instead of the present Lamp-tax, and hi order to enable the Land-Treasury to defray the heavier expenses, connected with the repairs & c. of those principal streets, that are publicly lighted at present, or to which lighting may in future be extended, shall

he paid : One eighth of the tax of 4 per Cent of the rent of all houses and lots in the above mentioned streets, to be collected together with said tax first time for the year 1854. One fourth of the Store-tax of all public stores or shops in the same streets, to be collected together with the Store-tax from the 1st of August 1854. 4. For each horse in St. Thomas shall be paid an annual tax, as follows : a, for a horse kept in town, $4, h, for a horse kept in the country, $1J. f>. For carriages in town not exclusively intended for transport of goods, an annual tax shall he paid as follows : a, for a four-wheeled carriage, $ 12, b, for a two-wheeled ditto, $ 8. From this rule however, such carriages are exempted, that notoriously have not been in use tor the last G months previous to the time the Tax is due.

6. For each vessel belonging to the Island of St. Thomas, and which is not of a tonnage making it li able to take out Sea-pass, an annual tax shall lie paid as follows: a, for a deck or half-deck boat with oi without a small boat (yawl), $4, b, for a sail boat without deck, $2, c, for a row-boat, $1, d, for a boat kept to supply ships with water, $10, e, for a launch or lighter or other similar vessel, used for the transportation of merchandize in the harbour, 10 dollars. 7. The Taxes to the Land-Treasury mentioned in 1, þÿ4 6, shall be paid on the 1st of January and the 1st of July, each time with the half amount, the first timeonthe 1st of January 1855 ; the Store-tax, according to 1 , however only for 5 months from the 1st of August 1854. To the Editor of thr " St. Croix Avis." Sir, The official list of the drawn numbers in the Cuban Lottery of the 24th ultimo arrived here yesterday, and, as usual, was a source of disappointment and vexation to many of my acquaintances, who invariably devote a portion of their limited means to the purchase of tickets in the Cuban and Porto Rican Lotteries ; and are always losers to a considerable, perhaps, injurious extent. Among the unsuccessful speculators in lottery tickets, there are many of
3 as,

opinion, that the numbers from the Spanish Colonies sent abroad are seldom or never put in th e'1 wheel" when the drawing is to take place, and that their frequent disappointments to are this measure attributable in a great circumstance. I cannot concur in their opinion ; but of this 1 am almost certain, that it has a weighty influence on the minds of the uninitiated, and unless we are sometimes allowed, through a fair process, to draw prizes ot some magnitude, there will be no inducement nor means to purchase tickets ; people that are poor will be likely to remain so; lottery tickets will ere long be spoken of as " things that were;" the Colonial Council will find it unnecessary to interfere with the introduction and sale of foreign lottery tickets; and in its future sittings will be the better able to display its ablility and zeal in matters of greater importance. Ere 1 conclude, permit me, Mr. Editor, to tender my thanks for your kind reception of my former communications; and in behalf of those whose pleasing anticipations are invariably destroyed by reference to the official drawings of the Spanish Lotteries, I beg leave to tell the Dons, that if they have made up their minds to keep their Prizes at home, we cannot much longer afford to purchase their Blanks. More when required. Meanwhile, I am, Mr. Editor. Respectfully, # #

Wo have had a long spoil of dry weather ; but from the frequent gathering ofheavy clouds, vve prognosticate a speedy change, which will be most timely and favorable. Although unprncticcd in the various stages of the planting process, yet we are confident that tin early season of rain is always necessary in our climate to the establishing of every young crop. A considerable portion of the present crop will have been reaped by the end of this month, which is already far advanced, and if we do not obtain seasonable showerr. the present as well as the ensuing crop must eventually suffer. It is our lot, however, to he visited yearly with a spell of drought, and in expectation of this annual visitor, the inhabitants of these islands generally find it obligatory on them to build reservoirs or cisterns for the preservation of water þÿ that essential of life. It is not unfrcquently the case that those who have not this convenience for retaining water in the rainy season, are placed in the greatest strait, and are compelled to purchase at a dear rate this indispensable article. Public cisterns in a climate like ours are rendered, by this peculiar feature, particularly valuable to the community, and might afford no insignificant source of revenue. A splendid cistern is erected on the Protestant Quay ; but we believe t hat it has been of very little value to the town since its erection, either as a source of revenue to the Treasury, or as a convenience for water in the dry
season of the year, in consequence of
iT18. its locality. We know that it was built at great expense, ana with a good a motive, no doubt, which has, however, fallen short of its end.

Very Interesting from þÿMexico. Where is Santa Anna? ( From the New York Herald J The Mexican news which we publish to-day very is interesting and curiows, the peculiarly significant feature of it being the sudden and mysterious departure of Santa Anna from his capital. Where has bis Serene Higlinessgone ? What for? When wijl lie return, or will he return at all ? These were the exciting questions which at the last accounts were agitating and perplexing all parties in the city of Mexico. It is reported, on the one hand, that the Dictator, with a detachment of his army, had gone off" to bant up those intractable rebels, Alvarez and Morenos þÿ that he had come up with the latter, had defeated him and captured him ; and had followed tip this triumph by putting Alvares himself to flight. This news, however, is supposed lo be equivalent to the Tartar report of the taking of Sebastopol ; or, at best, but a ruse of Santa Anna to cover up some ulterior purpose best known to himself. Another report assigns as the cause of his departure, Ins declining health. The city of Mexico, although in a deep, broad valley, is still some seven thousand feet above the level of the sea, and during the winter season is comparatively cold and damp. His Serene flighcause, superadded to " the cares of tless is said to be suffering from this State," and that lie goes down to the terres calientes, or hot lands of the southwestern departments, for the restoration of his health, leaving, ad interim, a sort of regency behind him in charge of the

government. Then, again, it is conjectured that this movement of the old fox is hut a device preparatory to a return to his capital, with a coup d'etat abolishing the republic entirely, and formaljy proclaiming the empire. But there is another conjecture concerning this mysterious journey of the Dictator, which, it appears, was pretty generally credited by intelligent men at Vera Cruz and Havana ; and it is this þÿ that Santa Anna having secured all the available funds of the Gadsden treaty, and other loose odds and ends, has left his capital, not for the purpose of putting down Alvarez, nor for the benefit of his health by sojourn near Acapulco, nor for an imperial coup d'etat, hut for the deliberate and judicious ultimatum of securing his head and his spoils by a timely farewell to Mexico, and a trip to Havana, preparatory to a summer visit with his interesting family to the Crystal Palace Exhibition of Paris. Now we venture to say that this conjecture is just a. likely to he confirmed as any other, in reference to this mysterious affair. The Mexican correspondence which we publish from the New Oilcans Delta, embraces some very curious facts and circumstances tending to corroborate the suspicion that this so- called Saviour of his Country," is now " resolved to save himself, and is slipping off for "Cowes and a market." A week or two will probably settle the question. Should it turn out by his turning up in Havana or Jamaica, or some other place, with his family and a ship load of plun-
der, that he has abdicated, absconded, and forever relinquished his rebellious subjects in disgust, then we may count upon n reaction in Mexico of the very

highest importance to us, and the balance of power on this continent. In any event, the crisis is fast approaching when the issue must he between a European protectorate, or the absorption of our sister republic by the United States. It would not be surprising if we were next to hear of the Dicl tatorfrom Kingston or Havana. It is evidently his best policy to pack up and pack off before his Gadsden spoils are exhausted. What an opening is here for the Kinney expedition ! Yellow Fever Prevented by Inoe ulaliou. We notice in La Cronica, that Dr. W m. L. Humboldt has discovered a means to prevent yellow fever, by inoculation. The Government of Cuba, as La Cronica is informed, has directed the inoculation of the major part, amounting to one thousand, of the newly arrived troops, which lias resulted in the greatest success, since none have been attacked by this terrible disease, which generally decimates the foreign population shortly after their arrival. The operation is similar to vaccination, by inserting the virus discovered by Dr. Humboldt, generally in both arms. A few hours after this trifling operation, the symptoms of a miniature yellow fever commence, and all the pathological consequences follow rapidly and slightly, rearly exceeding forty-eight hours in duration, and with nothing more than a slight feverish action. " We talk of Adam and Eve as having been, before the fall, in a very happy condition," says the Albany Register; " hut one tiling they missed þÿ they were

never bles. He never played ' hookey. children! Adam never played mar- ' He never drove a tandem of hoys with a string. He never skated on a pond, or played 'hall,' or rode down hill on a hand-sled. And þÿEve she never made a playhouse ; she never took tea with another little girl, from the tea-table set out with the tea-things. She never rolled a hoop, or jumped the rope, or They ' pieced Fussy wants a corner,' or hurly-burly,' never a bahy-quilt, or dressed a doll. played ' blind-man's huff,' or or any of the games with which childhood disports itself. " How blank their age must have been, wherein no memories of early youth came welling up in their hearts; no visions of childhood floating hack from the long past ; no mother's voice chanting a lullaby to the ear of Fancy, in the still hours of the night ; no father's words of kindness, speaking from the church-yard where he sleeps. Adam and Eve þÿ and they alone, of all the countless millions of men and women that have ever lived þÿ had no childhood !" The man who " earns his bread before he eats it;" who while procuring the means of ample subsistence for himself and family, is at the same time benefiting the community in which he lives, will peruse tho following, as all readers should do, with an acknowledgement of the woll-expressad truths which it contains : " The noblest men I know on earth, Are men whose hands are brown with toil , Who, backed by no ancestral graves, Hew down the woods, and till the soil, And win thereby a prouder name

Than follows kings' or warriors' fame." " The working men, whate'er their task, Who carve the stone or bear the hod, They bear upon their honest brows The royal stamp and seal of God , And worthier are their drops of sweat " God bless the noble working men, Than diamonds in a coronet Who rear tho cities of the plain ; Who dig the mines, who build tho ships, And drive the commerce of the main : God Have wrought the glorv of all lands bless them 1 for their toiling hand "

IIEAT 1 1 OF A FEMALE MISER. Some time ago, Miss Hall, a spinster, aged (56, distinguished by her miserly habits, closed her miserable career at Sheffield, leaving to the Girls' Charity School of that town between £5,000 and £6,000, amassed by a life of penury. In 1812, about which lini. her father died, she received a legacy of £100 under her grandfather's will. It was immediately after the acquisition of this sum of money that Miss Hall first manifested those quent penurious hahits for which Her life was remarkable. her subse- penury led her thus early in her career to discard soap as an unnecessary appendage of her toilet, and she boasted that she had not used any fur thirty years. Her only income was the interest on £100, and her own earninirs by making farm labourers' smockfrocks hut she contrived not only to live out of this, hut to save money. In connection with another woman she coinoienc.eil a system ul lending money out at interest, through the medium of Guinea Clubs, and this proved so profitable that in five or six years she was able to commence lending on mortgage of small lots ot cottage properly. The shutters of the lower rooms of her liou«e were barricaded, and she liv (I alone in the garret a miserable and wretched life, hut every year increasing her habits of penury and her hoard ol wealth. Coals she never bought, and frequently she sat for days together in the <b pili of winter without fire. Miss Hall, although she would literally starve herself to death rather than part with

her money, had no objection to a good dinner at any other person's expense, and during the last 10 or 15 years of her life she followed out a system by which she secured herself a good dinner and tea every day in flic week, except Sundav, tree of charge. This class of f'i iends she propitiated by promises to remember lliem in her will. To none ot these persons, however, has she left more than £10 Her attire was a "thing of shreds and patches." On her feet she usually wore a pair of cast-off mail's hoots, which were tied round lu-r ankles with strings. She had worn a bonnet for more I ban thirty years. Summer or winter, she wore pattens and carried an umbrella. Iler habits were very filthy. On a search being made at the house of the deceased three wills were discovered, all in her own handwriting, an I another drawn up by a solicitor in 1849, in all of which she left Iter property to the charity school. There was also found mortgage deeds, Midland Railway shares, debenture bonds of the Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway, and hankers' deposit notes, in all those It is believed hv amounting to £4.300. who knew her that it will ultimately he found that she died worth from £6,00(1 to 7, 000. These securities were found secreted in bundles of rags, tied up in old shirts, and some of the more portable ones, such as the hank deposit notes, were packed away in pieces of rags, inside old shoes, &c. In one box she had accumulated between fifty and sixty pieces of soap of different kinds, evidently the
contributions of friends anxious for her sanitary improvement. The interment took place at St. Philip's Church, and drew together some thousands of people.

au At the city of San Domingo an attempt at Revolution was tried, the object it would seem being for the recal of its exiled and ex-President Buena Ventura Baez. A body of men, composing about one hundred, is said to have collected in a large building within the city on the night of Sunday, the 25th u 1 1 . , and were awaiting the gathering of a like number ; their purpose was to attack the sentinels at the different gates, surprise the guards, þÿ whom they hoped to subdue, and then raise the cry of f iva þÿ Buena Ventura Baez! which they believed on the city becoming awakened would have been echoed every where. It would, however, seem that there was a traitor in the camp, who communicated to the Commandante the secrets of the plot, and towards midnight a body of soldiery surrounded the house and fired a volley of musketry into it ; the inmates frustrated attempted to make their escapes from the windows and doors, in doing which many captures were made, and the parties are now in prison to answer tor their acts. It is further said that several of those who escaped took refuge at the British Consulate, where they still continue to remain. President San Anna issued a Proclamation announcing to the Dominican people what had transpired, and quiet and order are said to again i reign in the country.
